title: AI Strategy for Business Leaders
subtitle: Decide where AI will pay off in your organisation, prove it with a well-designed pilot, and adopt it with the right data, governance and people in place.
outcomes: Explain in plain terms what machine learning and generative AI can and can't do for a business
Find AI use cases in your organisation's tasks and decisions, and prioritise them by value, feasibility, data and risk
Decide whether to buy an AI product, build on a model through an API or build your own
Design a pilot with a baseline and success criteria, and work out its return on investment honestly
Set up governance that fits the risk, and lead the people side of adopting AI
prerequisites: None: no technical background is needed. You need a spreadsheet program (Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc) for two of the labs. It helps to have an organisation in mind: your own, or one you know well.
description: Every organisation is being told to do something with AI. This course helps leaders do the right things, in the right order. You'll learn what machine learning and generative AI can and can't do, in plain terms; find use cases in the tasks and decisions of your own organisation and prioritise them by value, feasibility, data readiness and risk; decide whether to buy a product, build on a model through an API or build your own; and design a pilot that gives a clear answer, with an honest calculation of its return. The last module covers what makes AI adoption last: risk management and governance in proportion to the stakes, and the skills, roles and communication that bring people with you. The labs are done on paper and in a spreadsheet, with a sample textile manufacturer or your own organisation, and the course ends with an AI strategy you write for an organisation you know.

modules.title: What AI can and can't do for a business
modules.summary: Cut through the hype: what machine learning and generative AI actually do, where they're strong, where they fail, and why an AI strategy starts with business goals rather than technology.

lessons.title: AI, machine learning and generative AI in plain terms
objectives: Explain how machine learning differs from rule-based software
Describe the main kinds of task AI systems perform
key_points: Traditional software follows rules that people write; machine learning systems learn patterns from examples in data, so they can handle tasks too fuzzy for hand-written rules, such as spotting fraud or reading handwriting.
Most business machine learning is predictive: it estimates a number or a category from data, such as next month's demand, the chance a customer leaves or whether an invoice is a duplicate.

Generative AI models, such as the large language models behind chat assistants, produce new text, images, code or audio by predicting what is likely to come next, from patterns learned from very large amounts of data.
AI systems give probable answers, not guaranteed ones: every model makes some mistakes, so the useful questions are how often, how badly and who catches them.
Most useful AI tasks fall into a few families: predicting, classifying, recommending, detecting anomalies, extracting information from documents, and generating or summarising content.

lessons.title: Where AI is strong, and where it fails
objectives: Identify the conditions in which AI tends to work well
Recognise common failure modes, including hallucination, drift and bias
key_points: AI works best on frequent, well-defined tasks with plenty of relevant examples and a clear way to tell a good result from a bad one.
Large language models can state false information fluently and confidently, which is called hallucination, so their outputs need checking wherever accuracy matters.
A model learns from the past: when customers, markets or processes change, its accuracy can quietly fall, which is called drift, so models need monitoring after launch.
Models can repeat and amplify patterns in their training data, including unfair ones, such as favouring the kinds of applicants who were hired in the past.
AI can't be accountable: decisions that matter to people, money or safety need a human owner who understands the system's limits.

lessons.title: Strategy first: tie AI to business goals
objectives: Explain why an AI strategy starts from business goals
Describe the main kinds of value AI can create
key_points: An AI strategy is part of the business strategy: it says which goals AI will serve, where it will be used first, and what the organisation needs in data, skills and governance to get there.
Starting from a problem worth solving, such as slow quotes or frequent stock-outs, works better than starting from a technology and looking for somewhere to use it.
AI creates value in four main ways: growing revenue, cutting cost or time, reducing risk, and improving the experience of customers or staff.
Much of AI's value comes from improving parts of existing processes, such as drafting, checking or forecasting, rather than from replacing whole jobs.
A good strategy also says what the organisation won't do, such as fully automating decisions about people, and how progress will be measured.

lab.title: Map AI opportunities to your business goals
lab.goal: Connect three of an organisation's goals to tasks where AI could help, and test each idea against what AI can and can't do.
setup: An organisation you know well: your own, a former employer or a business you use often
A document, a spreadsheet or a sheet of paper

steps.do: Write down three business goals for the next year or two, each with a measure, labelled Goal 1, Goal 2 and Goal 3. For example: Goal 1: cut the time to send a quote from three days to one.
For each goal, list the tasks people do today that affect it. Look for tasks that are frequent, repetitive, data-heavy or slow.

Pick the one task per goal where AI could help most. Label it Task:, and add a line AI task type: naming its family (predicting, classifying, recommending, detecting anomalies, extracting information, or generating or summarising content).
Add a line Could go wrong: saying what a mistake would look like, how often it might happen and who would notice.
Add a line Owner: naming the role that stays responsible for the result, and whether a person checks every output, some or none.
Finish each goal with a line Verdict: saying whether AI is worth exploring for it, and why. At least one verdict may well be no.

checks.text: Three goals are given, each with a measure.
Each goal has one task, matched to a family of AI task.
Each task says how it could go wrong and who would notice.
Each task has a responsible owner and a level of human checking.
Each goal ends with a reasoned verdict.

lab.submit: Paste your three goals, each with its Task, AI task type, Could go wrong, Owner and Verdict lines.
hints: If you can't say how you'd measure a goal, it's too vague to plan AI for: make it specific first.
A task where a mistake is costly and hard to spot needs a person checking every output, which reduces the time saved.

modules.title: Finding and prioritising use cases
modules.summary: Find candidate uses for AI in tasks and decisions, score them for value, feasibility, data readiness and risk, and check that the data can really support the best ones.

lessons.title: Finding use cases in tasks and decisions
objectives: Find AI use cases by breaking work into tasks and decisions
Gather ideas from the people who do the work
key_points: Look for use cases in tasks, not whole jobs: a job is a bundle of tasks, and AI usually helps with some of them, such as drafting replies or checking documents.
Good candidates happen often, follow a recognisable pattern, use information already held digitally, and cost time or money when done slowly or wrongly.
Mapping a process step by step, with the people who do it, shows where time goes, where errors creep in and where decisions wait for information.
Repeated decisions made with data, such as which leads to call, how much stock to order or which claims to check, are classic places for predictive AI.
Front-line staff often know the best opportunities and the hidden pitfalls, so workshops and interviews with them beat ideas chosen only by senior leaders or vendors.

lessons.title: Scoring value, feasibility and risk
objectives: Score use cases against consistent criteria with weights
Sort use cases into quick wins, big bets, fill-ins and ones to avoid
key_points: Scoring every idea against the same criteria, such as value, feasibility, data readiness and risk, makes choices comparable and the reasoning visible.
A weighted score multiplies each criterion's score by a weight for its importance and adds them up; the weights are a judgement, so check whether changing them changes the ranking.
On a value-feasibility grid, quick wins are high on both, big bets are valuable but hard, fill-ins are easy but worth less, and ideas low on both are usually dropped.
Feasibility includes having the data, the skills and the systems to connect to, not only whether the technology exists.
Risk covers harm to customers or staff, legal and regulatory exposure and damage to reputation; a high-risk idea needs stronger safeguards, not only a lower score.

lessons.title: Is your data ready?
objectives: Assess data for relevance, quality, access and permission to use it
Spot data problems that would sink a use case
key_points: Data readiness means data that is relevant to the task, of good enough quality, accessible to the people and systems that need it, and allowed to be used for this purpose.
Quality has several dimensions: accuracy, completeness, consistency across systems, timeliness and, for supervised learning, reliable labels that record the right answer.
A predictive model needs enough historical examples of the outcome it predicts, including the rarer cases, such as defaults or defects, that often matter most.
Under data-protection laws such as the EU's GDPR, personal data needs a lawful basis and a purpose compatible with why it was collected; licences and contracts can restrict other data too.
Generative AI tools that answer from company documents depend on those documents being current, findable and correctly permissioned, or they'll repeat outdated or confidential information.

lab.title: Prioritise an AI backlog in a spreadsheet
lab.goal: Score eight candidate use cases for a textile manufacturer, rank them, place them on a value-feasibility grid, and test how much the ranking depends on the weights.
setup: A spreadsheet program: Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc
Download use_cases.csv and open it in your spreadsheet

steps.do: Open use_cases.csv. Each use case is scored from 1 to 5 for value, feasibility, data readiness and risk, where 5 is always best: a 5 for risk means the lowest risk.

In G1 type Score, and in G2 enter a weighted score with weights of 40% value, 30% feasibility, 20% data and 10% risk. Copy it down to row 9. If your spreadsheet uses a comma as the decimal separator, separate arguments with semicolons and write 0,4 for 0.4.
steps.see: 4.4 for UC1, the raw-material demand forecast.

steps.do: Sort rows 2 to 9 by Score, largest first (Data | Sort in Excel and LibreOffice Calc, Data | Sort range in Google Sheets), keeping the header row out of the sort.
steps.see: UC1 (4.4), UC4 (3.9) and UC7 (3.7) at the top.

steps.do: In H1 type Grid, and in H2 label the use case Quick win (value and feasibility both 4 or more), Big bet (value 4 or more, feasibility under 4), Fill-in (value under 4, feasibility 4 or more) or Avoid (both under 4). Copy it down.
Test the weights: in I1 type Value-heavy, and in I2 score the use cases again with 60% value, 20% feasibility, 10% data and 10% risk. Copy it down and note which use cases move.

Write a line starting Top three: naming the three use cases you would pursue, then a sentence for each on why, including one risk you would manage. You don't have to follow the scores blindly; say where you depart from them.

checks.text: The weighted scores are right: UC1 4.4, UC4 3.9, UC7 3.7, then UC2 3.5, UC6 3.4, UC3 3.3, UC5 2.8 and UC8 2.4.
The grid labels are right: only UC1 is a quick win, UC3 and UC4 are big bets, UC2, UC6 and UC7 are fill-ins, and UC5 and UC8 are ones to avoid.
The value-heavy scores are right, and the submission notes that UC3, the fabric-defect check, rises to third (3.6) above UC7 (3.5).
Three use cases are chosen, each with a reason and a risk to manage.

modules.title: Build, buy or use an API, and proving the value
modules.summary: Choose how to get an AI capability, then prove it: a pilot with a baseline and agreed success criteria, and an honest calculation of the return.

lessons.title: Build, buy or use an API
objectives: Compare the main ways to get an AI capability
Ask vendors the questions that reveal cost and risk
key_points: Buying a product with AI built in, such as forecasting in a planning tool or an assistant in an office suite, is usually the fastest way to start, but you get the vendor's features and roadmap.
Using a model through an API, such as a large language model from an AI provider, lets you build your own application on a capable model without training one, usually paying for what you use.

A model can be adapted by grounding its answers in your own documents (retrieval-augmented generation) or by fine-tuning it on your examples; for questions about company knowledge, grounding is usually tried first.
Building a custom model gives the most control and can be an advantage when your data is unique, but it needs data, specialist skills and ongoing maintenance.

Ask every vendor how your data is used (including for training their models), where it's stored, what evidence shows the product works on cases like yours, what it costs at full scale and how you would leave.

lessons.title: Designing a pilot that gives a clear answer
objectives: Design a pilot with a hypothesis, a baseline and success criteria
Use a comparison group to separate the AI's effect from other changes
key_points: A pilot is an experiment: it tests a hypothesis, such as 'extracting invoice data with AI cuts processing time by half without more errors', in a limited, time-boxed setting.
Measure the baseline before the pilot starts, and agree success criteria and stop criteria in advance, so results aren't reinterpreted afterwards to suit whoever backed the project.
A comparison group working without the AI over the same period separates the AI's effect from seasonal swings, new staff and other changes.
Measure quality and risk as well as speed: error rates, complaints, customer satisfaction and how often people override or correct the AI.
Choose pilot users who represent normal working conditions, not only enthusiasts, and plan who will own the system, and pay for it, if it succeeds.

lessons.title: Measuring return on investment
objectives: Estimate the total cost of an AI system
Calculate return on investment and payback period, and test their assumptions
key_points: Return on investment (ROI) is net benefit divided by cost, (benefit − cost) ÷ cost, shown as a percentage over a stated period such as the first year.
Total cost includes licences or usage fees, integration, data preparation, training, monitoring and support, and the staff time to run the system, not only the software.

Time saved is a financial benefit only when it turns into something of value, such as more work done, less overtime or fewer hires, so count the share you can realise, not the full theoretical saving.
Payback period is how long the net benefit takes to cover the one-off costs; with steady benefits it's the one-off cost divided by the net benefit per month.
Test the result by changing key assumptions one at a time: if the case only works under the most optimistic ones, it's fragile.

lab.title: Work out a pilot's return
lab.goal: Turn an invoice-extraction pilot's results into a first-year return on investment and a payback period, then see how much they depend on one assumption.
setup: A spreadsheet program: Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc
Download pilot.csv and open it: the pilot's results and costs, in made-up figures in any currency

steps.do: Open pilot.csv. Column B holds the values: 30,000 invoices a year, 6 minutes each before the pilot and 2 minutes with AI (checking and correcting what it extracts), and the costs.
In column D type these labels in D2 to D9: Hours saved per year, Value of time saved, Realised benefit, One-off costs, Running costs per year, First-year cost, First-year ROI, Payback (months).
In E2 to E4 work out the benefit. Only half the time saved is expected to turn into value (B6), because the rest is absorbed into other work.
In E5 to E7 work out the costs: the one-off costs, the running costs (the per-invoice fee plus monitoring and support) and the total for the first year.
In E8 work out the first-year ROI and format it as a percentage with one decimal place. In E9 work out the payback period in months.
Copy the results somewhere safe, then change B6 to 0.25, as if only a quarter of the time saved were realised, and read the new ROI and payback.
Write a short recommendation, starting Recommendation:, on whether to scale up, and which assumption you would check first and how.

checks.text: The payback period is right: 7.2 months.
The costs include the one-off costs (13,500) as well as the running costs (7,500 a year).
With only a quarter of the time saved realised, the ROI falls to -28.6% and payback stretches to 21.6 months.
A recommendation says whether to scale up and which assumption to test first.

lab.submit: Paste your labels and results from column D and E for both runs (with B6 at 0.5 and at 0.25), then your recommendation.

The ROI is negative at 0.25 because the first year carries all the one-off costs; the case for later years can still be positive, so say which period you're judging.

modules.title: Risk, governance, people and change
modules.summary: Manage AI's risks with governance in proportion to the stakes, and bring people with you: skills, roles and honest communication decide whether AI is adopted or quietly ignored.

lessons.title: The risks of AI in business
objectives: Describe the main kinds of AI risk
Match risks to safeguards
key_points: Key AI risks include inaccurate outputs, unfair treatment of groups of people, leaks of personal or confidential data, security attacks, intellectual-property disputes, breaking laws and damage to reputation.

Generative AI adds its own risks: confident but false answers, prompt injection (instructions hidden in content that trick a system into misbehaving), and staff pasting confidential data into unapproved tools.
Risk depends on the use, not only the technology: the same model is low-risk drafting internal notes and high-risk deciding who gets a loan or a job.
Safeguards include human review before outputs are used, testing for accuracy and bias, access controls, logging, clear policies and the ability to switch a system off quickly.

Existing laws on data protection, consumer protection and discrimination already apply to AI, and some places have AI-specific rules too, such as the EU's AI Act, so check what applies where you operate.

lessons.title: Governance that fits the risk
objectives: Set up the basic building blocks of AI governance
Scale oversight to the risk of each use
key_points: AI governance is how an organisation decides, documents and oversees its uses of AI: who may approve what, under which rules, and how problems get found and fixed.
The basic building blocks are an AI policy, an inventory of the AI systems in use, a risk assessment before new uses go live, named owners and regular review.
Proportionate governance gives low-risk uses a light, fast route and saves detailed testing, review and sign-off for high-risk ones.
Published frameworks can give governance a structure, such as the voluntary NIST AI Risk Management Framework from the US and ISO/IEC 42001, a certifiable standard for AI management systems.
An acceptable-use policy tells staff which AI tools they may use, with what data, how to check outputs and how to report problems.

lessons.title: People, skills and change
objectives: Plan the skills and roles that adopting AI needs
Lead change in a way that builds trust
key_points: Adoption decides value: a tool that people don't trust, or don't know how to use, delivers nothing, however good the pilot results were.
Everyone who uses AI needs basic AI literacy (what it does, where it fails and how to check it), and some roles need deeper skills, such as prompt design, data work or overseeing models.
Be honest about how roles will change: involving staff in redesigning their work, and saying clearly what happens to the time saved, reduces fear and resistance.
Change models such as ADKAR (Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement) remind leaders that people need to understand why, want to take part, learn how, practise and see the change last.
Champions in each team, quick ways to give feedback, and leaders who visibly use the tools themselves help new ways of working stick.

project.title: Write an AI strategy for an organisation
project.brief: Write a short AI strategy (three to five pages, or a deck of about ten slides) for an organisation you know, or for the textile manufacturer from the labs. Connect AI to the organisation's goals; choose and justify a small portfolio of use cases; assess data readiness and decide how to get each capability; plan a pilot for the top use case with a baseline, a comparison group, success and stop criteria and an estimate of its return; and set out the risk, governance and people plan that will make adoption safe and lasting. Write for a busy executive team: plain language, clear choices and honest numbers.
deliverables: A one-paragraph summary of the strategy for executives
Three to five prioritised use cases, with their scores and the reasoning behind the ranking
A data-readiness assessment and a build, buy or API decision for the top use case
A pilot plan: hypothesis, baseline, metrics, comparison group, success and stop criteria and timeline
A return estimate with first-year ROI, payback period and at least one sensitivity test
A risk and governance plan, and a people and change plan

rubric.name: Tied to business goals
rubric.description: Every use case serves a named goal with a measure, and the strategy says what the organisation won't do as well as what it will.

rubric.name: Choice of use cases
rubric.description: Use cases are scored on consistent criteria, the ranking is explained, and the effect of the weights is tested.

rubric.name: Data and sourcing
rubric.description: Data readiness is assessed with evidence, and the build, buy or API decision compares the options on cost, control over data, fit, skills and how to leave.

rubric.name: Pilot and return
rubric.description: The pilot has a baseline, a comparison group and success and stop criteria agreed in advance; ROI and payback are calculated correctly from total costs and realisable benefits, and tested against a key assumption.

rubric.name: Risk and governance
rubric.description: The main risks are named with safeguards and owners, and oversight is in proportion to the risk of each use.

rubric.name: People and change
rubric.description: Skills, changes to roles and communication are planned honestly, with a way for staff to give feedback.

project.submit: Paste your strategy (or the text of your slides), including your scoring table and your ROI calculation with its assumptions.
